Linux Container in 500 Lines of Code

summary.title: Linux containers in 500 lines of code
summary.one_liner: Learn how Linux containers are built from kernel primitives (namespaces, capabilities, cgroups, rlimits, seccomp) by reading a small annotated C program that runs untrusted code in a restricted process tree.
takeaways: Containers combine namespaces (mount, pid, ipc, net, uts, user), capabilities, cgroups, rlimits and seccomp; each is a separate kernel mechanism that overlaps with the others.

The author's program clones a child into new namespaces, sets up cgroups and a hostname, optionally maps uids via a user namespace, drops a list of risky capabilities, and filters syscalls before execve.
Dropping capabilities requires clearing the bounding and inheritable sets, because execve could otherwise restore them from file capabilities.

Some capabilities (e.g. CAP_SYS_ADMIN, CAP_SYS_RAWIO, CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH, CAP_MKNOD) are dangerous inside containers because they are not namespaced; the article explains why each is dropped or kept.
The author stresses this is a minimal restriction set for running untrusted code, not a recommended production setup; real deployments should restrict everything possible.
summary.summary: Lizzie Dunham's literate-programming article walks through a roughly 500-line C program (contained.c) that runs a shell inside a restricted Linux container. It is written in noweb style, with code blocks assembled into the final source. The article explains each mechanism in turn: namespaces created via clone, a uid mapping through user namespaces, cgroups and setrlimit limits, seccomp syscall filtering, and a detailed justification for each capability dropped or retained. It is explicit that the restrictions are a minimal set for untrusted code rather than a complete hardening guide.
